en: Having bowed to the glorious Hayagrīva, who holds in his four hands the conch, the discus, the book, and the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), I shall explain here the difficult-to-understand meanings of that which was spoken by Nārada.
In this system, the vowels are counted in order as follows: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au. (Note: *ḷ* and *ḹ* are included here as per the specific tradition mentioned).
It has been determined that those [sections] which begin with *kaṭa* and so forth are to be excluded from the *yogārṇava*.
Furthermore, an *anuvāka* situated here is counted as such by its own internal connection;
a sentence joined with other letters or beginning with a *yuga* (pair of syllables) does not constitute an *anuvāka*. 3.
In a *yoga*, that which is the second [vowel] and that which follows it constitute a single *vākya*;

even if they belong to the same class (*savarṇa*) or the same group (*savarga*), there is no *yoga* between them in that case. (4) For *ma*, *da*, *ga*, *ta*, and *sa* with a bindu (*anusvāra*), there shall be increases of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, and fifty [respective units]. (5)
This technical terminology of Nāradabaiṭa, which is difficult for even the wise to understand,
was composed by the son of Śrī Rāma for the sake of understanding the meaning of the Baiḍa;
this technical terminology is intended for the easy comprehension of children.

I shall now further clarify this by means of the "Cakra" (Wheel). Regarding the phrase *anṛvarṇapluta*: here, in this *Ānandabhairava*, *anṛvarṇaplutalṛkārāḥ* refers to those vowels (*ac*)—namely the vowel *ṛ*, the protracted vowels (*pluta*), and the vowel *lṛ*—which are not present [in certain positions]. The meaning is that they are distinct from the protracted *a*-vowel, the protracted *i*-vowel, the protracted *u*-vowel, the *ṛ*-vowel, the *ṝ*-vowel, and the *lṛ*-vowel. Such vowels—the vowels beginning with *a* and so forth—are counted in sequence. Starting from the first, the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *au* constitute one [group].

The meaning is that they are counted in the sequence of two, three, four, five, and so forth. "Conjunct letters" (*saṃyogavarṇāḥ*) refers to those letters formed by conjunction. Keśava states: "Both *arṇa* and *varṇa* denote letters in the context of writing. Thus it has been said by the learned: "In the wheel of the syllables of the Gāyatrī, there is a smiling lotus with petals numbering sixty-four. This means the consonants (*vyañjana*) that have become conjuncts. Those conjunct letters occur in groups such as *ka-ṭa* and *ka-ṭa-pa-ya*, and so forth.

The meaning is that [the letters] beginning with *ka*, *pa*, and so forth, should be counted according to their numerical sequence. The syllable *na* is to be excluded, as it signifies absence; the meaning is that it is to be understood as zero (*śūnya*). Thus it is determined: the meaning of these technical conventions has been established in summary.
(8) He further elaborates upon this very meaning stated in the summary with the words beginning with "saha" and so forth. (9)

Regarding the word *saha* (together): here, in this context, the negative particle *na* is used; by that, [it means] "by this. By the letter *n*, [it means] "together with" (*sārtham*). "That which is standing and this" means "standing" (*sthita*) and "not standing" (*asthita*). By that, [it means] "with the standing and the not-standing vowel. This means "with the vowel standing after the letter *n*. A section (*anuvāka*) is counted. This means that sections such as "iṣe tvā," "yajñasya śundhaddhvam," "karmaṇe deva," and so forth, are counted. Not joined with another phoneme (*nānyavarṇayujā*).

"Non-other" (*nānya*) means other than the letter *na* (*nakārāt anyaḥ*). "Non-other letter" (*nānyavarṇaḥ*) means a letter other than the letter *na*; that is to say, a consonant distinct from the letter *na*. "Joined with that" (*tena yuk*) means joined with a letter other than [the letter *na*]. By that, [it is] "joined with a non-other letter" (*nānyavarṇayujā*). "With a vowel" (*acā*) means with a vowel characterized by a letter other than the letter *na*. A sentence is counted [as a single unit]. Examples: *ubhārādhasassahamādayaddhyai*, *sā tayehuve vām*, *utavāghāsyālāt*.

The meaning is that [the sections] ending with the various sentences found within those respective *anuvākas* are counted. Regarding "by the beginning of a *yuga*" (*yugādinā*): here, the conjunction of two consonants is called a *yuga*. Its beginning is the "beginning of a *yuga*" (*yugādi*). By that "beginning of a *yuga*"—meaning by the first letter of a conjunct—[the *anuvāka*] is counted. The meaning is that the *anuvākas* such as "indrāgnī," "omāso," "marutvantamindram," "marutvo," "marutvān mahān," and "mahān nṛvat" are counted. 10

Regarding the term *yoga*: in a *yoga* (conjunction) consisting of two conjunct consonants (*saṃyuktavyañjana*), that which is the second—the second consonant—[is the cause]; and by that second letter, as well as by what follows it (*tatparāc*). "That which follows it" (*tatpara*) means that which comes after that second consonant; thus, "by that which follows it" (*tena tatparācā*) means even by the vowel that follows it. The meaning is: "even by the vowel following [the second consonant]. *Vākyakam* is simply *vākya*. It is counted. Herein, this is the meaning.

The meaning is that even with a consonant following a conjunct (*saṃyoga*), the very end of a sentence situated in the middle of a recitation (*anuvāka*) is also counted as such by means of the subsequent vowel. Furthermore, he states "not homogeneous" (*na savarṇaḥ*) because here, for the two consonants constituting a conjunct, what is intended is their lack of homogeneity (*asavarṇatva*) and their non-belonging to the same class (*asavargīyatva*). In that case, even regarding the two letters in a conjunct, there would be no homogeneity or belonging to the same class with the following vowel; therefore, that conjunction—the union of the two consonants—would not be homogeneous nor belong to the same class. 12.

Regarding the phrase *modogotassabindu*: *mo* is the letter *ma*; *do* is the letter *da*; *go* is the letter *ga*; *taḥ* is the letter *ta*; *saḥ* is the letter *sa*. These letters, when accompanied by the nasal dot (*bindu*), constitute the "increases by ten" (*daśottaravṛddhi*). The meaning here is that starting from the letter *ma*, each subsequent one increases by a factor of ten in its numerical position. In this context, the meaning is that they should exist in sequence with the nasal dot (*sabinduka*) as follows: *maṃ* in the place of ten, *daṃ* in the place of twenty, *gaṃ* in the place of thirty, *taṃ* in the place of forty, and *saṃ* in the place of fifty. Thus, they should be formed in this order with the nasal dot. 13.
This *Nāradabaḍartho*, difficult to grasp even for the wise, has been thus clarified by that learned Cakrin for the delight of scholars.
(14) Thus ends the commentary on the *Nāradabaḍaparibhāṣā*.
This commentary on the *Baiṭa* composed by the sage [Śaṅkarācārya], known as the *Bhāvaprakāśikā*, was made by that Cakrin.

The *Bhāvaprakāśikā*, [a commentary] by the son of Śrī Rāma, is completed. Om. For the sake of the crops, thee! In the new Veda, O thou who art ever-new and unwearied in speed; in the waters that are ever-new, devoid of flaws, and flowing; in the forest-dwellers, the radiant ones, the shining ones, the hearers, the Indra-like ones, the sleepless ones, the scatterers, the destroyers, and the weavers; do not weep! Do not sound a cry, O thou who art never-decaying and never-failing! O thou whose arms are all-pervading and whose nature is unyielding! O thou whose face is like a new-born moon and who art free from disease! O thou who art the navel, the formidable one, the one joined with the earth, the one possessing light, the one who causes the earth to flourish, and the one who is the source of the world! The first book (*prathamakāṇḍa*) is completed.
Vāyavyaṃ naugū | One should bury it. Novīnigū | Nīmnajumunude | Nau nadu | Nau gaigi | The second section is completed.
Prajāpati desired.

We speak with a voice free from cavities; we do not speak with a voice that is uneven or crooked; we have not spoken with a voice that is distorted. We have not spoken with a voice that is devoid of breath, nor with a voice that is harsh. The third *kāṇḍa* is completed.

Yoking first [the mind], he has reached the goal through the *maighuda*, the *didima*, and the *mogomeda*. He has established the end of the *dida*; he has taken hold of the *godīmeda*. He is the one who bestows the *nimana-viṣa-nido-bhuṣī*. He is the one who is not to be surpassed by men. He is the one who knows this path. He is the one who has attained the *gigidaida-ga*; he has bestowed the *godudada*. In the light, he is the one who has reached the summit. The fourth *kāṇḍa* is completed.
He offers the *sāvitrāṇi* oblations:
"nauda" (1), "naumama" (2). The [mantras] for the third and fourth questions do not appear [in the text]. "nūbhānābhānene" (5), "dūnau naina" (6), "namebhīvainalūmovīvīnene" (7).
[He approaches] the *prācīnavaṃśa* hall.

And in the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth questions, there are no *lakṣya* (target) words: 5. *nūthanī*, 6. *prajananam jyotiḥ*, *nuvanī-bhānu-vanā*. 1. In the second [question], there are no *lakṣya* words: 2. *naumuna-bhune*, 3. *ne ne bhunavaimagāronā*, 4. *nūthanaivābhānūbhāna*. 5.
Thus ends the seventh book.
Salutations to the Supreme Brahman, who is affectionately disposed toward His devotees.
